zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical coverage was cross-checked against the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0). This is a lexical aid, not a substitute transcription; the supplied BnF scan remains the authority. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

runs.text: i, toda a fazenda, ou herança. ¶

lines.note: Continues the final Ixxeqi entry on f277: all one’s property or inheritance. The following Japanese example starts Ixxe- and continues on the next row; the italic i, is an explanatory marker within the Portuguese continuation, not a new Japanese headword.

runs.text: qini fanaruru. l, ixxeqiuo mexi fanaſa-

lines.note: Completes Ixxeqini fanaruru and gives an alternative passive expression involving the removal of one’s estate. The final mark after fanaſa is a raised horizontal hyphen, not the draft period; ruru follows on the next physical line.

runs.text: Ser priuado de todos ſeus bens aßi mo-

lines.note: Ruru completes the Japanese passive on the previous row. The Portuguese explains being deprived of all one’s property, both movable and landed; mo- is the beginning of the word completed as uis below.
Uis completes mo-uis, movable goods, contrasted with landed property. The new example means to hand over or bequeath the whole estate; the scan ends yuzzuru with a period, not a hyphen.

runs.text: Dei xar a alguem todos ſeus bens.

lines.note: Explains the bequest example: leave all one’s property to someone. The unusually separated Dei xar is kept as printed/aligned rather than silently collapsed; its meaning is the verb deixar.
A new Ixxeqi, paraphrased as Fitotçuno muxiro, means one mat. This is distinct from the estate sense carried over from f277.
Ixxet, equated with iſſai, is an adverb meaning “in no way” when combined with a negative. Enlargement supports e in the historical joined form Denehũa, not the OCR c; quã- begins the next word.

runs.text: do ſe ajunta com negatiuo. Vt,

lines.note: Do completes quã-do, and the explanation specifies combination with a negative. The Japanese example begins Conofoni-; the faint vowel outlines are retained without adding an unattested length mark, and the rest follows below.

Uoite completes the opening phrase begun on the previous row; the example denies any difference or change on the speaker’s part. The damaged opening is read uoite rather than the OCR noite, consistent with its surviving strokes and the Japanese construction. Emmim starts the translation.

runs.text: naõ hà outra couſa, l, mudança. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Continues “in me there is no other thing, or change.” The printed naõ and the vel marker l, within the Portuguese are retained; Item begins a further adverbial meaning.
Gives the further affirmative/general senses of Ixxet: totally or in any event. The whole row belongs to the same adverb entry.
This separate Ixxet means a piece of news or a report. Its example Ixxetga qicoyeta says that a report has been heard, with the Portuguese translation on the following row.
Translates the preceding example as “a report is circulating/sounding.” The scan reads Soa, not the OCR Sda; hũa noua refers to a piece of news.
Ixxi, paraphrased as Fitorigo, means an only child. The Portuguese Filho vnico and its historical initial v are preserved.

This Ixxi denotes a single line or thread. The initial headword letter is I, not long ſ. The paraphrase is retained as Io fitoſugi: only a small ink remnant lies between I and o, where Ito would be expected; a full t is not securely recoverable, so this damaged reading remains a nonblocking caveat.
Ixxi, Fitoyeda, means one branch. The repeated headword represents a different counted object, not a duplicate of the preceding thread entry.
Ixxi, Fitotçuno yubi, means one finger. The Japanese paraphrase and Portuguese Hum dedo agree.
Ixxi is one sheet of paper, paraphrased Cami ichimai. Cami here is part of the ordinary Japanese headword explanation, not a word embedded in Portuguese prose.

The example urges extending charity even in the amount of a sheet of paper or half a cash coin. The Portuguese translation begins with A. and continues inda below; the dot-like terminal mark is retained rather than automatically converted to a hyphen.

runs.text: inda que ſeja couſa muito pouca como hũa folha

lines.note: Inda completes the preceding A. as the concessive ainda: even though the gift is very small, like a sheet of paper. The physical division and its unusual preceding punctuation are preserved.

runs.text: de papel, ou mea caxa não deixeis de dar

lines.note: Continues the charitable-giving example with paper or half a cash coin and the injunction not to withhold giving. Caxa is the historical coin term in this context, not an ordinary box.
Eſmola completes the injunction: do not fail to give alms, even a very small gift. The single-word row closes the example under the paper-sheet sense.
A further Ixxi means a written document, such as an acknowledgment or receipt. The scan has capital I; conhecimento is used as the name of a document here, not abstract knowledge.
The examples Ixxiuo toru and daſu mean taking or issuing such a document. The Portuguese translation begins Tomar and continues with its alternative on the next row.

runs.text: ou dar eſte papel como conhecimento.

lines.note: Completes the examples’ explanation: take or give this paper as an acknowledgment. It remains part of the written-document entry.
This Ixxi concerns one death or dying once, paraphrased Fitotabi xiſuru. The Portuguese alternative morrer is physically divided after mor, without adding a hyphen absent from the aligned scan.

Rer completes mor-rer in sense, although the row is printed with close rerhũa spacing. The example Ixxi ſaiquat xezu states that one who has died does not come back to life; O q̃ begins its translation.

runs.text: morre hũa vez não torna a viuer, ou reſuſcitar

lines.note: Continues the statement that someone who dies once does not live again or rise again. The final letter of hũa is a, not the draft t; the next row adds the important qualification naturalmente.

Naturalmente qualifies the entire statement about not returning to life: it concerns the natural course of events. The qualification is retained as part of the dictionary’s own gloss, not dropped from the meaning note.
Ixxin, Fitorino voya, denotes one parent, either father or mother. The printed Portuguese pay and mãy are preserved.

This Ixxin means one body, substance, or one person alone. The paraphrase is retained as Fitotçuno ma because the damaged final letter does not securely show i; mi would fit the meaning, but that expectation does not justify silently replacing the visible/aligned a. Subſtã- continues on the next row.
Cia completes subſtã-cia, then the gloss adds “one alone.” The example Sonoaidani ixxin begins a narrative illustration of a person acting alone, continued below.

Completes the Japanese example: the person dug a hiding hole alone. Taif. Lib. begins a citation whose book number is 32 on the next row; the roman citation name and italic Lib. remain distinct as in the scan.

runs.text: Entre tanto elle ſò fez hũa coua em que

lines.note: The opening 32 completes the preceding book citation. The Portuguese says that meanwhile he alone made a pit in which he could hide; the purpose clause continues below.
Completes the hiding clause, then gives Ixxindeua narumai, saying that the speaker cannot manage alone. Eu starts the new translation and joins the following row.

Completes “I alone, by myself, shall not be able.” The damaged word after por is adopted as mĩ: the final character bears a nasal mark, while part of the m has lost ink. This replaces the unusable draft nã; the damaged m remains a documented caveat rather than a claim of perfect legibility.
A separate Ixxin, paraphrased as one pillow, is glossed Hũa almofada. The final S. is the upright usage label, distinct from the italic Portuguese gloss.
This Ixxin means one heart or mind, paraphrased Fitotçuno cocoro. Its example below develops the sense of wholehearted concentration.
Ixxin iccǒni negǒ means wishing wholeheartedly and single-mindedly. Both o marks in the Japanese example open upward as carons, and the explanation continues below.

runs.text: inteiramente ſem ſe diuertir em outras couſas.

lines.note: Completes the wholehearted-wishing gloss: entirely, without turning one’s attention to other things. Diuertir here concerns distraction or diversion of attention, not primarily amusement.

Ixxinpuran and ixxinfuran are alternative forms for strong attention or single-minded devotion. The printed close punctuation around .l, is retained; the activities to which the attention is applied follow below.

runs.text: & deuação, com que hum lee algum liuro, re-

lines.note: Continues with the devotion used when someone reads a book or prays. The scan supports lee algum liuro, correcting the draft le algumu luro; re- is the beginning of reza on the following row.
Za completes re-za, “prays,” followed by &c. The short row ends the list of activities performed with devoted attention.

Ixxinpuranni is the adverb: attentively and devoutly. The headword is followed by a visible comma rather than the draft period; deuo continues into tamente below without supplying a conjectural terminal hyphen.
Tamente completes deuotamente. The Japanese example describes someone being in an attitude or appearance of concentrated devotion, translated on the next row.

Translates the example as showing much devotion and attention. The damaged beginning is adopted as Moſtraua: faint tall remnants precede the surviving t, rather than a clear c as in the OCR. The exact long-s/t impression remains a nonblocking graphic caveat.

Ixxiqi, paraphrased Fitotçuno iro, denotes one kind of things. The scan supports the initial Ixxiqi, iro with r, and plural couſas; the draft Faxiqi, Fatocçuno ito, and singular couſa are corrected. The next column begins a distinct sense of the same headword.

runs.text: O entender, ou fazer ſoo. Vt,

lines.note: A distinct sense of Ixxiqi concerns undertaking or doing something alone, independently. The example begins Ix- with capital I, not lowercase l; its continuation follows on the next row.
Xiqini ſuru completes Ixxiqini ſuru, acting independently or at one’s own discretion. The Portuguese begins doing or handling some thing, divided as cou-ſa across the row boundary.
Completes “a thing according to one’s own will,” then begins Ixxiqini tocorouo xiru. The next row supplies the verb and explains independent governance of a place.

runs.text: Gouernar por ſi ſoo algum lugar.

lines.note: Xiru completes the example, glossed governing some place by oneself alone. The Portuguese Gouernar, por ſi ſoo, and lugar agree with the exercise of independent control.
Ixxit is one loss or mistake, paraphrased Fitotçu vxinǒ. The following example contrasts a wise person’s occasional loss with a fool’s occasional gain.

runs.text: Chixaua xenrioni xite canarazu ixxit ari;

lines.note: First half of the proverb: even a wise person, in a thousand deliberations, necessarily has one mistake. The scan’s final punctuation is a semicolon after ari, not an extra s in the draft aris.

runs.text: guxaua xenrioni xite canarazu ittocu ari.

lines.note: Second half: even a foolish person, in a thousand deliberations, necessarily has one gain or success. The terminal mark after ari is a period, not the draft hyphen.

runs.text: O prudente, & ſabio de mil couſas que

lines.note: Xix. is the roman source label attached to the preceding Japanese proverb. The italic Portuguese translation begins with the prudent and wise person considering a thousand things; it continues below.

runs.text: conſidera hũa ſoo erra, o ignorante de mil hũa

lines.note: Continues the contrast: the wise person errs in only one of the thousand matters considered, while the ignorant person gets one right. The second clause reaches its final verb on the next row.

Completes the proverb’s translation: the ignorant person gets just one right. The printed separation a certa is retained; in context it functions as acerta, rather than an unrelated feminine adjective phrase.
Ixxǒ, Fitotçuno naricuxe, denotes one nature or disposition. The glossary marks it as Buddhist terminology on the next row; nature- is the beginning of natureza.
Za completes nature-za. The damaged upright label is read Bup., the dictionary’s Buddhist-term marker, not Bap.; the same label with a similarly weak u occurs later in this column.
Ixxô, Fitotçuno xôco, denotes a testimony or witness statement. The circumflexes are visible in both Japanese forms and distinguish this entry from surrounding caron-bearing spellings.

This Ixxǒ means an entire lifetime. The example Ixxǒ fubon concerns lifelong chastity; the full Portuguese Toda a vida is italic, rather than leaving its initial T outside the italic run as in the draft.

runs.text: ſtidade perpetua, ou de toda a vida. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes Ca-ſtidade: perpetual chastity, or chastity for one’s whole life. The damaged d of ſtidade is retained within the word, correcting the draft separation ſtida le; Itẽ introduces a further sense.
Adds the sense of one and the same birth or parentage. The example Ippucu ix- begins here and continues with xǒno qiǒdai, brothers/siblings of the same parents.

Completes Ippucu ixxǒno qiǒdai. The Portuguese identifies siblings born of the same father and mother, with the parent terms on the next row; both long-o marks in this Japanese continuation are carons.
Pay, & mãy completes the sibling definition: the same father and mother. This does not introduce a new parent entry.

This Ixxǒ means one bed or cot, paraphrased Fitotçu toco. Enlarged comparison supports the short crossed t in catre rather than the OCR carre. The o mark in the headword is weak, so the aligned caron is retained without claiming that its two arms are equally clear.
Ixxǒ, paraphrased as one clan or lineage, means a family or generation. The Portuguese word reads familia, not famitia; gẽ- continues as ração on the next row.
Ração completes gẽ-ração, the lineage or generation sense. It closes the family entry before the next Ixxô.
The example Ixxô ichinen concerns concentrated invocation, with the explanation beginning “to invoke intensely.” Inten is physically continued by ſa below without a supplied line-end hyphen.

Completes the explanation: invoke the name of Fotoque intensely and attentively. Fotoque is a roman Japanese term within the Portuguese sentence, followed by the upright Buddhist usage label Bup.; these are not all one italic run.
This Ixxô is one laugh. The initial letter is I, not long ſ; the final S. is the separate written-usage label rather than part of the Portuguese noun phrase.

Ixxǒ is paraphrased as Fitocoye, a single cry or utterance, but the Portuguese is retained as Hũa vez. The vowel in vez is open/worn, and the aligned e reading is not securely disproved by enlargement; the expected voice sense is recorded as a nonblocking mismatch, not silently substituted as voz.
Ixxo, Fitotocoro, means one place. The example beginning Ixxo describes a monk without a fixed place of residence, completed on the next two rows.
Fugiǔno ſô completes the Japanese phrase for a monk who does not settle in one place. The Portuguese calls him a bonzo who is always wandering or on pilgrimage; pere- continues below.
Grinando completes pere-grinando, and the gloss adds that the monk has no fixed home. This is the itinerant-monk illustration of Ixxo, not a separate entry.
Another Ixxo means a letter, paraphrased Fitotçu caqu. The example Ixxouo mochij ſoro is divided after Ixxo, whose particle and verb follow on the next row.
Completes the letter-writing formula and translates it as “I write this letter.” No begins the regional alternative on the next row; the entire Portuguese word is italic, including its final o.

In Cami the dictionary gives the alternative formula Ixxouo motte mǒxi ſoro. Cami is a Japanese regional name inside the italic Portuguese apparatus and is marked for whole-word font review; the final S. is the upright written-usage label.

runs.text: Não morar em hum lugar certo.

lines.note: Ixxo fugiǔ means not residing in one fixed place. The following row points back to the earlier Ixxo entry containing the itinerant-monk example.
Vide, Ixxo is the cross-reference completing the preceding entry. Ixxo is an embedded Japanese cross-reference term following the Portuguese/Latin apparatus word, not a new main headword on this row.
Ixxǒgai is equated with Ixxeno aida and glossed as the whole of one’s life. The synonym following i, remains ordinary Japanese synonym text and is not added to typeface_terms.

runs.text: Hum corpo darmas inteiro, ou eſ

lines.note: Ixxǒzocu denotes a complete suit of armour or a complete outfit. The Portuguese also begins eſquipação at the right edge, divided after eſ without a conjectural hyphen; the long ſ and adjacent rule are both visible in the crop.
Quipação completes eſ-quipação in sense, followed by clothing, good ornaments, and so on. The printed spelling veſtidos and the complete list remain on this row.
Ixxǔ, one xǔ, means one religious sect. The scan reads ſeita with i and t rather than the OCR ſenta; the two Japanese u marks are carons.
Ixxucu, Fitotomari, denotes a single night’s lodging. The example on the next row turns this into the act of staying for one night.
Ixxucu ſuru is explained as lodging or taking shelter, with the duration hũa noite on the next row. The printed spacing agaſalhar ſe is preserved.
Hũa noite completes the lodging example’s duration: one night. It closes that sense before the armour entry.
A separate Ixxucu is equated with Ixxǒzocu and denotes a complete suit of armour. The Portuguese adjective inteiro continues below.
Completes the full suit of armour and gives Ixxucu yorô, to arm oneself fully. The o in yorô has a visible circumflex, not the draft caron; the Portuguese idiom continues below.
De ponto em branco completes the idiom for being fully armed/equipped. The row ends the I-before-X section; the heading below is furniture, not part of this gloss.

IY, paraphrased Mexi, means cooked rice. The enlarged initial I belongs to this row and extends beside the following row; the draft omitted it and recorded only Y. The two-row initial is represented explicitly in the line attributes and crop.

Iy, yǔ, yǔta is the verb paradigm for speaking or saying. Its ordinary initial I is distinct from the lower portion of the enlarged I to the left, which belongs to the preceding rice entry; the caron-marked u forms are preserved.

Iya is glossed “no.” The draft’s extra leading l and Nôo misread the left rule/initial and the Portuguese nasal vowel. The second Iya at the far right is a separate catchword, now removed from the body text and retained in its own furniture zone.
